title: Bavan Akhri close
hook: a long alphabet ending in grace

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart of the Bavan Akhri: letters learned without the Name stay empty. Your line was learning with heart. What did you learn yesterday that reached past your head? Day one thousand two hundred two.

A school slate at the end of the day. Chalk dust in the corners, a row of letters copied over and over, a teacher's mark at the bottom. Guru Arjan's Bavan Akhri in Raga Gauri works like a slate, stretched across the pages of the Guru Granth Sahib from Ang two hundred fifty. Letter after letter, each one opens a lesson. For two days we've walked inside it. Today we reach the bottom of the slate, where the teacher leaves the last mark. And the last mark isn't a grade. It's a gift.
screen: `A SLATE AT THE END OF THE DAY.` → `LETTER AFTER LETTER.` → `THE LAST MARK IS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: An acrostic sets up an expectation. Each letter is a step, and steps sound like effort: learn this, then this, then this, and you'll arrive. The Bavan Akhri uses that shape, and along the way it says hard things, like the sassa stanza's warning about cleverness that goes nowhere. You'd expect the ending to be a reward for the student who finished every letter. Instead, as this path reads it, a long alphabet ends in grace. In that reading, the close turns from the student to the Giver: the Name comes through the Lord's mercy and the Guru's kindness, not through anyone's own cleverness. That turn has a name in Sikh vocabulary. Kirpa is mercy, kindness given freely. Nadar is the gracious glance, the Lord looking with favor. Sikh teaching holds both together with effort. Sikhs are asked to rise, remember, work honestly, serve. And Gurbani speaks of the fruit of all that as a gift. Some readers hear the whole composition as a lesson in the right order of things. First you learn your letters. Then, having learned them, you find out who was holding the chalk. So the long schoolroom poem doesn't end by praising the pupil. It ends with the pupil looking up. That's worth carrying out of a lesson that long: the work was real, and the gift was bigger than the work.
screen: `AN ALPHABET SOUNDS LIKE EFFORT.` · `THE CLOSE TURNS TO THE GIVER.` · `KIRPA AND NADAR.` · `WHO WAS HOLDING THE CHALK?` · then, large: `ENDS IN GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read its last stanza. If you have a gutka, an app or a printed Guru Granth Sahib nearby, find the closing lines of the Bavan Akhri in Raga Gauri and read them once, slowly, in Gurmukhi or in translation. If you don't have them to hand, sit with one thing you worked hard for this year, and notice how much of it was also given: a teacher, a chance, a person who said yes. Hold both, the work and the gift. If you pray, you can say Waheguru quietly as you close. The bell holds the time.
Bavan Akhri close. Guru Arjan's alphabet of lessons, which ends by turning from the pupil to the Giver. Today's word.
Your line: ends in grace. Today, when you finish something, a task, a meal, a hard conversation, take one breath to notice what was given to you along the way. Day one thousand two hundred two.

howItsDone: The Bavan Akhri of Guru Arjan is part of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Gauri; some Sikhs read it through in their own study or hear it explained in katha at the gurdwara.
